title: Wind farms and the people who see them

turns.speaker: Deshi
turns.text: The offshore extension got approved in about nine months. The onshore one up the valley has been in planning for six years.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: Offshore nobody lives next to, which is most of the explanation.

turns.speaker: Moira
turns.text: It's also three times the price per unit, and that gets left out when people say offshore solved it.

turns.speaker: Moira
turns.text: It's narrowing, but onshore wind is still the cheapest thing you can build in this country by some distance.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: The objections aren't irrational, though. Someone's view does change, and telling them the planet needs it doesn't address what they actually said.

turns.speaker: Deshi
turns.text: The Danish approach is the one that interests me. Local people are offered a share in the thing, so it becomes an income rather than an imposition.

turns.speaker: Deshi
turns.text: Opposition drops dramatically when the turbine pays your community's bills.

turns.speaker: Moira
turns.text: Which sounds like a bribe to a certain kind of objector.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: Or like compensation, which is a normal feature of infrastructure everywhere else.

turns.speaker: Moira
turns.text: That's the better framing, yes. A motorway pays for noise barriers and nobody calls that a bribe.

turns.speaker: Deshi
turns.text: The bird argument keeps coming up too, and the numbers are worth knowing. Cats kill orders of magnitude more.

turns.speaker: Ana
turns.text: Although siting matters. A turbine on a migration route is a different case from one in a field.

points: An offshore wind extension was approved in nine months while an onshore scheme has taken six years.
Ana attributes the difference to proximity to residents.
Moira notes offshore costs around three times as much per unit, and onshore remains the cheapest generation available.
Ana argues objections about changed views are reasonable and not answered by appeals to climate need.
Deshi cites the Danish model of local ownership, which sharply reduces opposition by turning the project into income.
They agree compensation is normal infrastructure practice, and note bird deaths are far lower than from cats, though siting on migration routes matters.
